Why AI researchers warn humanity could face extinction
Thomas Latschan
7 hours ago7 hours ago

Could artificial intelligence pose an existential threat to humanity? Some leading researchers are warning against an unregulated race toward AI superintelligence.
https://t.co/zSJPy5RElw
Copy link
A symbolic image of an AI robot at the Mobile World Congress 2024
Some researchers argue that artificial general intelligence could pose unforeseeable risks
Image: Marc Asensio/NurPhoto/IMAGO

Dramatic warnings about the existential risks posed by artificial intelligence to humanity are nothing new.

As early as the 1940s, the renowned scientist and science fiction author Isaac Asimov explored potential risks and unintended consequences of intelligent machines.

In 1991, Hollywood blockbuster "Terminator 2" imagined a dystopian 2029 in which an out-of-control military AI called Skynet directs killer robots in a war against humanity.

If the warnings of several of the biggest names in AI are to be believed, a similar scenario could become a reality — even before 2029.
Hollywood actor Arnold Schwarzenegger as TerminatorHollywood actor Arnold Schwarzenegger as Terminator
The opening sequence of 'Terminator 2' depicts a dystopian future where AI has spiraled out of control and turned against humanity
Image: Columbia/dpa/picture alliance
Growing calls for strict regulation

"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," AI researcher Jacob Coxon posted on X last week, without exactly explaining how it might happen.

"No other human activity poses this level of danger," he added.

Coxon also revealed that he had quit his job at Anthropic, a US-based AI company, in protest against what he saw as an irresponsible race among AI companies to develop an ever better, self-improving superintelligence.

He warned that algorithms could begin to analyze and improve their own source code independently, which could shrink development cycles from several months to just a few minutes and thus make them uncontrollable.

Coxon is not an isolated voice. Nobel Prize-winning physicist Geoffrey Hinton, often called the "Godfather of AI," has been warning for years about the serious consequences of artificial superintelligence.

In 2023, he left his job at Google to publicly warn of the dangers of AI technologies he helped pioneer. Yoshua Bengio, a pioneer of artificial neural networks and deep learning, has also expressed concern about current developments and called for government regulation.

As recently as July 2026, more than 1,000 employees of leading AI companies warned in an open letter of an imminent loss of control if the race for "superintelligence" were not subject to significantly stricter regulations.
Caught in an unregulated race?

Despite the growing warnings, US President Donald Trump's administration has clearly shifted its AI policy toward minimizing regulatory hurdles and accelerating AI development.

In his X post, Jacob Coxon indirectly criticized the consequences of this policy: "At OpenAI, many have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes. At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first — they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk." 

Coxon, who had moved from OpenAI to Anthropic in early 2026, is familiar with both corporate cultures.

In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, he said that under the "most aggressive scenarios," things could spiral out of control as early as the end of 2027.
America's AI boom: Who pays the price?
12:34

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, for his part, is currently calling for a coordinated, industry-wide slowdown in development to buy time to address the risks and prevent any misuse of AI.

In a lengthy essay shared on X over the weekend, he wrote that in six to 12 months, AI agents "could be capable ​of taking over the entire internet" and potentially cause "hundreds of billions of dollars in damage" without proper guardrails.

Both Elon Musk, who runs xAI, and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, said they agree with Amodei.
The alignment problem

In recent years, numerous experts have voiced concern about the rapid AI advances, particularly the development of artificial general intelligence, which refers to systems that not only solve individual tasks but also match or exceed human intellectual capabilities in nearly all areas.

Sophisticated AI models, for instance, may pursue goals in ways that diverge from human intentions, something AI security researchers refer to as the "alignment problem."

On top of that, even developers can't always fully understand how AI makes certain decisions.

And so, it's no surprise that Coxon's former colleague Evan Hubinger came to his defense.

"Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," Hubinger, who himself is the team lead for alignment stress tests at Anthropic, wrote on X.

In his post, Hubinger made clear that Anthropic hasn't yet found a solution to the alignment problem and warned that an AI model might begin to resist being shut down, because that would limit its ability to achieve its programmed goal.
Exaggerated hysteria?

Other AI experts, however, consider such doomsday scenarios to be extremely unlikely.

Among the most prominent critics of the so-called AI doomers is Meta's chief scientist, Yann LeCun. In October 2024, he dismissed such concerns as "complete nonsense."

Still, other experts note that developing AI systems requires enormous amounts of computing power, energy, data and infrastructure.

They argue that an AI model cannot simply take over the world because it would need to rely on servers, power grids, communication systems and physical resources that are controlled by humans.
China's humanoid robots put to the test
12:34
Does the real danger lie elsewhere?

In fact, many experts see the short-term risks not so much in the extinction of humanity as in the numerous indirect consequences of AI systems that already exist even without superintelligence.

These include disinformation campaigns on an unprecedented scale and the related manipulation of democratic processes, an expansion of mass surveillance, and job losses across numerous industries.

Just last week, Anthropic revealed that there had been several attempts by users to misuse its Claude AI models for research that could support biological weapons development. The company said it had banned the accounts involved.

In August, Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI caused a stir when they announced that their AI systems had unintentionally carried out autonomous hacking activities.

Following reports of further AI hacking attacks during testing, even top US AI frontier labs are now expressing a willingness to slow down the development of the technology.

Why a Character Sheet Matters in AI Video Generation:  

A character sheet locks the character’s identity, appearance, outfit, and key details—keeping every shot visually consistent from start to finish. 

 Created with  @ChatGPT 
Character Sheet Prompt :

Use the uploaded reference image as the SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH for the character.

Create a highly realistic, professional cinematic CHARACTER SHEET based on this exact reference character.

IDENTITY LOCK:
Preserve the character's exact facial identity, facial proportions, eye shape and color, eyebrows, nose, lips, jawline, skin tone, freckles/skin marks, hairstyle, hair color, apparent age, and overall recognizable appearance.
Do NOT redesign, beautify, age, de-age, or change the character's identity.
The same person must look unmistakably identical in every panel.

OUTFIT & DESIGN LOCK:
Accurately reproduce the exact clothing, colors, materials, patterns, jewelry, shoes, accessories, hairstyle and other visible design elements from the reference image.
If a detail is not visible, infer it conservatively and keep it consistent with the visible design.
Do not introduce random costume changes.

CREATE A PREMIUM PROFESSIONAL CHARACTER SHEET WITH THIS EXACT STRUCTURE:

1. PRIMARY PORTRAIT
- One large cinematic close-up portrait
- 3/4 or front-facing composition
- Clearly show face, hair, skin texture and outfit details
- Natural realistic expression
- Photorealistic skin and hair

2. FULL-BODY CHARACTER VIEWS
Create three matching full-body views side-by-side:
- FRONT VIEW
- SIDE VIEW
- BACK VIEW

Keep the exact same character identity, hairstyle, proportions, body type, outfit and accessories across all three views.
Full outfit must be clearly visible from head to toe.
Maintain realistic anatomy and consistent proportions.

3. EXPRESSIONS
Create 5 close-up facial expression panels of the SAME character:
- NEUTRAL
- SMILE
- SERIOUS
- LOOK AWAY
- EYES CLOSED

Only change facial expression and eye direction. Facial identity must remain perfectly consistent.

4. DETAIL SHOTS
Create 4 clean close-up detail panels showing the most important character design elements:
- CLOTHING / NECKLINE DETAIL
- SLEEVE / ACCESSORY DETAIL
- WAIST / OUTFIT DETAIL
- FABRIC / MATERIAL DETAIL

Choose the actual most visually important details from the reference image if the outfit differs.

5. PHYSICAL DETAILS
Add a clean professional information panel containing:
- AGE RANGE
- HEIGHT
- BODY TYPE
- SKIN TONE
- HAIR COLOR
- HAIR STYLE
- EYE COLOR
- DISTINCTIVE FEATURES

Only include information visually supported by the reference. Do not invent specific facts unnecessarily.

6. COLOR PALETTE
Create a professional color palette section with circular swatches and labels for:
- PRIMARY OUTFIT COLOR
- SECONDARY OUTFIT COLOR
- SKIN TONE
- HAIR COLOR
- EYE COLOR
- LIP / ACCENT COLOR

Include accurate HEX color codes sampled/estimated from the reference.

7. ACCESSORIES
Show clean close-up detail shots of the character's important accessories such as:
- NECKLACE
- EARRINGS
- BRACELET
- RINGS
- HAIR ACCESSORIES
or whatever accessories are actually present.

VISUAL STYLE:
Premium fashion character-sheet presentation, photorealistic cinematic photography, Netflix-level realism, luxury fashion editorial quality, natural skin pores, realistic hair strands, physically accurate fabric, realistic shadows, subtle depth of field, sophisticated neutral studio/interior background.

LAYOUT:
Create one polished professional character-sheet board containing all sections in a clean organized grid.
Use thin elegant dividers, subtle off-white/cream panels, professional typography, clear section headings and small labels.
Match the visual organization and presentation quality of a high-end film/character design reference sheet.

CONSISTENCY:
The character must be EXACTLY the same person throughout the entire sheet.
No identity drift.
No face variation.
No hairstyle variation.
No outfit variation.
No random accessories.
No inconsistent body proportions.
No duplicate/missing limbs.
No distorted hands.
No warped facial features.

OUTPUT:
Ultra-detailed, photorealistic, cinematic, professional production-ready character reference sheet, high resolution, sharp details, coherent lighting, realistic anatomy, consistent character identity across every panel.

Daily Young Trend Brief | September 12, 2026

A few signals moving across fashion, music, social media and creator culture.

1. Fashion is treating the past like a parts bin

NYFW is pulling from preppy, Americana, Y2K and older styling codes without committing to one period.

Skirts over pants, brooches on blazers, sweaters tied at the waist and extra-long necklaces are all showing up.

The effect is less period revival than remix. Older aesthetics are becoming components that can be recombined.

2. Beauty is getting deliberately less polished

Texture is creeping back into beauty.

Big hair, glossy red lips, blue eye makeup and partially crimped hair are appearing alongside loose twists and deliberately imperfect styling.

The everyday version will probably be simpler: one strong lip, one unusual texture or one detail left slightly undone.

3. K-pop is exporting the fandom system

Rock in Rio held its first K-pop-focused day, with Stray Kids headlining and lightsticks officially allowed inside the festival.

The surrounding culture traveled with the music: merchandise pop-ups, photocards, fanchants and coordinated lightstick participation.

K-pop exports songs, but it also exports an operating system for fandom.

4. Songs are turning into remix family trees

TikTok can revive an old track and then split it into remixes, dances, edits and new versions.

Tove Lo’s 2015 track “Talking Body” is a current example, resurfacing through a viral remix and dance trend more than a decade after release.

For creators, another question now sits alongside chart position:

Can this sound keep generating new formats?

5. Old memes are being resurrected with AI

“Remember November 2026” brought the old Polar Bear 2026 meme back through a strange AI-generated singing video.

Covers and edits followed.

The individual meme may disappear quickly. The production method probably will not.

Internet culture now has decades of old images, jokes and half-forgotten references that generative video can cheaply turn into new material.

The meme archive just became editable.

6. Algorithmic feeds are becoming a policy question

Australia is proposing that users over 16 should be able to opt in or out of algorithmic recommendation feeds.

That changes the framing.

The question is no longer only how good a recommendation system is. Products may increasingly be judged by how much control users have over whether recommendation is running at all.

Turning the algorithm off could become a product feature.

7. Athletes are becoming media companies

Elite athletes are building audiences, launching products and developing businesses alongside competition.

Sports organizations are adapting too, with creator programming moving closer to major events and athletes increasingly producing their own media.

The emerging career stack looks familiar:

athlete → audience → media → product

Creators reached this model early. Other professions are beginning to adopt it.

8. Foldables are no longer an Android-only experiment

Apple has unveiled the iPhone Duo, its first foldable iPhone.

For Korean consumers, folding hardware itself is already familiar. The next thing to watch is what Apple’s entry does around the device: app layouts, multitasking, accessories and content formats built for a screen that changes shape.

New hardware matters most when software behavior begins changing around it.

Today’s trend radar

heritage remix
controlled messiness
fandom infrastructure
remix culture
AI meme revival
algorithm choice
athlete-owned media
foldable software

The longer-cycle signals look stronger around fandom infrastructure, user control over recommendation systems and people turning audiences into products they own.

The individual meme, accessory or beauty detail can disappear next week.

Those shifts have more structural staying power.

The interesting part isn't the plugin. It's what powers it.
 
Six months ago we made an architectural bet. Build the entire ImagineArt tool layer as a single MCP server, and let every AI surface consume it. One backend. Many clients.
 
Today that bet pays off.
 
The same server that already powers ImagineArt inside @claudeai, @cursor_ai, @grok, and our CLI is what just shipped inside @OpenAI's ChatGPT. 50+ tools sitting behind one endpoint at https://t.co/ukyJJ9PCc6. Image generation, video, music, logos, ads, fashion shoots, editing, upscaling. All of it.
 
No forking codebases per client. No rewriting integrations. When we add a new model or a new tool, it lands on every surface at once. That is the entire point.
 
The engineering wins here are worth naming:
 
→ OAuth handled at the protocol layer, so no API keys ever ship to the user
 → Async job orchestration for long-running video and music generations
 → Multi-turn guided flows for Ads and Fashion that hold state across the conversation
 → Credit metering that works identically across every client, no per-surface accounting
 
MCP is going to be the HTTP of the AI era. If your product is a set of tools, ship it as an MCP server first. Everything else follows from that decision.
